story: The Rhode Island State House stands at 82 Smith Street, just below the crest of Smith Hill. It is Rhode Island's seventh state house and the second in Providence. McKim, Mead & White, a well-known New York firm, designed it, and it was built from 1891 to 1901.

The building uses 327,000 cubic feet of white Georgia marble, 15 million bricks and about 1,309 short tons of iron floor beams. Its dome is described as the fourth largest self-supported marble dome in the world. It was also one of the first public buildings to use electricity.

On top of the dome stands a gold-covered bronze statue, The Independent Man. It was first named Hope. George Brewster designed it, the Gorham Manufacturing Company cast it, and it was installed in 1899. It weighs more than 500 pounds. Inside, the State Room holds a full-length portrait of George Washington by Gilbert Stuart.
stops.fact: The statue on top was first named Hope.
stops.disputed: Many people think the dome is the biggest marble dome in the world. Wikipedia calls it the fourth largest self-supported marble dome.

The State House dome is the largest marble dome in the world.

story: The Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul is the mother church of the Diocese of Providence. Pope Pius IX created the diocese in 1872, and its first bishop, Thomas Francis Hendricken, decided to build a new cathedral because the first one was too small.

In 1873 Hendricken chose church architect Patrick Keely to draw the plans. The cornerstone was laid in 1878. Hendricken refused to borrow money for the project, so he set aside $10,000 each year and ran fundraising campaigns to keep construction going.
By 1882 the contractors had finished the roof and began the interior. Hendricken died in 1886. The Neo-Romanesque church was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1975.

story: The Van Wickle Gates are the ornamental entrance to Brown University's main campus, at the crest of College Hill. They were paid for by the bequest of Augustus Stout Van Wickle, Class of 1876, a bank president who died in 1898. He also paid for a set of gates at Princeton University.

Hoppin & Ely and Hoppin & Koen designed them in wrought iron with brick and stone piers. The Brown coat of arms crowns the gate, and the piers carry the seals of Rhode Island and Providence. The sides carry inscriptions by Cicero. They were dedicated on June 18, 1901.

The two small side gates stay open all year. The big center gates open only on special days: inward at the start of the school year and the start of spring semester, and outward for the Commencement procession.
stops.fact: The center gates open only on three days a year.
stops.disputed: Many people think the big gates are always open. Wikipedia says only the side gates are, and the center opens on three annual occasions.

The big center gates stay open all year.

story: The Westminster Arcade was erected in 1828 at 130 Westminster Street and 65 Weybosset Street. It is notable as the first enclosed shopping mall in the United States, and it is a fine example of commercial Greek Revival architecture. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1976.

Cyrus Butler developed it, and Russell Warren and Tallman & Bucklin designed it, with a lane of shops lit by skylights, like similar buildings in Europe. At first it was far from the shopping areas, so few customers came and it was known as Butler's Folly for many years. In June 1843 President John Tyler toured it and reportedly shook 5,000 hands.
It declined late in the twentieth century and was rehabilitated and reopened in 1980. It closed again in 2008 and reopened in October 2013 as shops plus small apartments called micro-lofts.
stops.fact: It was first called a folly.
stops.disputed: Many people think the first mall must be a modern idea. Wikipedia says this one was erected in 1828.

claims.t: The Arcade was busy with shoppers from its first day.
claims.why: Wikipedia says it was slow to attract customers and known as Butler's Folly.
